partial_case.facts: In July 2022 the resident reported a broken fence in her back garden to the landlord. Following her report the landlord attended to inspect, however, it did not complete repairs. The resident reported the need for a repair to the back fence to the landlord between 5 July 2022 and 7 February 2023. The landlord inspected the fence in November 2022 and February 2023. On 21 August 2023 the resident complained about the landlord's handling of the fence repair. She said she chased it for updates about the status of the repair. It informed her in August 2023, that the repair was not its responsibility. On 6 September 2023 the landlord sent the resident its stage 1 response. It said the maintenance and repair of the fence was the resident's responsibility. It stated information to this effect was in the resident's handbook. On 9 September 2023 the resident escalated her complaint. The resident referred the complaint to us and said she wanted the landlord to repair the fence.
partial_case.ground_truth_outcome: Service failure by landlord regarding fence repair response; no maladministration in complaint handling; £50 compensation ordered

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord reasonably set out that the resident was responsible for the repairs. It acknowledged it did not communicate to its expected standard as part of the process. However, despite identifying this was inappropriate, it did not provide any redress to put things right.

The landlord upheld the complaint because it failed to inform the resident from the outset that the fence repair was her responsibility to undertake. The landlord inspected the fence twice, which created false expectations and led to the resident to chase the repair for a year before the landlord confirmed its position that the resident was responsible for the repair under the tenancy conditions.

The landlord apologised to the resident for the lack of clarity about the responsibility to repair when she first reported the matter. An apology as a part of putting things right was appropriate but not proportionate on its own given the impact of its failure to clarify the repair responsibility sooner.

partial_case.facts: The landlord was London Borough of Redbridge and the occupancy was a secure tenancy. In July 2022 the resident reported a broken fence in her back garden; the landlord attended to inspect but did not complete repairs. The complaint was about the landlord's response to the fence repair and the investigation also considered complaint handling. The resident reported the need for a back-fence repair between 5 July 2022 and 7 February 2023, and the landlord inspected the fence in November 2022 and February 2023. On 21 August 2023 the resident complained about the landlord's handling of the fence repair and said she had chased for updates; she was informed in August 2023 that the repair was not the landlord's responsibility. On 6 September 2023 the landlord sent its stage 1 response stating that maintenance and repair of the fence was the resident's responsibility and that information to this effect was in the resident's handbook. The resident referred the complaint to the Ombudsman and said she wanted the landlord to repair the fence.

ground_truth_outcome.remedy: Landlord ordered to pay the resident £50 compensation

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord reasonably set out that the resident was responsible for the repairs. It acknowledged it did not communicate to its expected standard as part of the process. However, despite identifying this was inappropriate, it did not provide any redress to put things right.
The tenancy handbook states residents are responsible for maintaining fences and boundaries. The landlord’s complaint response was in line with this.
An apology as a part of putting things right was appropriate but not proportionate on its own given the impact of its failure to clarify the repair responsibility sooner.
The compensation ordered is in line with our remedies guidance, which recommends this amount would be suitable where a failure caused inconvenience, but did not change the overall outcome.
